slides.title: Hash Tables
slides.main: Insert, lookup and delete in constant time on average, however much data is stored.

captions: A key is any string, number or tuple
The hash function turns a key into an integer
The remainder mod table size is the slot index
We land on the spot with no scanning: constant time

body.text: Twenty exercises: your own hash function, your own table built several ways, and problems on top of it.

slides.title: Idea
slides.main: The slot index is computed from the key — no scanning needed.

captions: An array of eight slots: all empty so far
cat: hash % 8 = 1 — put the pair in slot 1
dog → 5, fish → 6: each key goes to its own slot
Find dog: same calculation — straight to slot 5, no scanning
A good hash function is deterministic, fast and uniform
Keys are multiples of 8, size 8: division dumps all 16 keys into one slot
Multiplication mixes: the same keys spread almost evenly

slides.title: String hash
slides.main: h = h · base + char code; a window hash updates in O(1).

captions: Characters are polynomial coefficients; start with h = 0
Each step: h = h · 31 + char code (modulo a large number)
Sliding the window by one character updates in constant time — the basis of Rabin–Karp

frames.text: window b c → h' = (h − code(a)·31²)·31 + code(d)

slides.title: Collisions
slides.main: Pigeonhole and birthdays: collisions are inevitable and frequent.

captions: More keys than slots — at least two share a slot
Even a nearly empty table collides often: with 100 slots, 13 keys give over 50% odds
You can’t avoid collisions — make them cheap: chaining or open addressing

slides.title: Chaining
slides.sub: Each slot holds a list of pairs
slides.main: Average chain length equals the load factor α.

captions: Each slot holds a chain of pairs; hash is the remainder mod 6
7 % 6 = 1, 14 % 6 = 2, 11 % 6 = 5: each key in its own chain
20 % 6 = 2: slot taken — append to the end of the chain
Look up 20: slot 2, then along the chain. Average length is the load factor

slides.title: Linear probing
slides.sub: Open addressing: everything in one array
slides.main: Simple and cache-friendly, but clustering needs a roomy table.

captions: 5 % 8 = 5: slot free — place it
13 % 8 = 5: taken — step to the next, 6
21 % 8 = 5: pass 5 and 6, land in 7
6 % 8 = 6: go 6, 7 and wrap to 0 — runs merge
Look up 29 (% 8 = 5): 5, 6, 7, 0 taken, 1 empty — no such key, five probes

slides.title: Deletion: tombstones
slides.sub: You can’t just clear the slot
slides.main: A tombstone doesn’t break the run; rebuilding discards tombstones.

captions: Keys 5, 13 and 21 sit in a row starting at slot 5
You can’t just clear the slot of deleted key 13
Find 21: slot 5 — not it, slot 6 empty — “no such key”? But it’s further on!
Tombstone ✕: lookup passes through it and finds 21
New key 29 (% 8 = 5) will take the tombstone’s place

slides.title: Quadratic and double
slides.main: Quadratic steps or a second hash spread the paths apart.

captions: Key with hash 3: steps of one slot — occupied ones merge into a run
Steps by triangular numbers: 3, 4, 6, 9 — key paths diverge quickly
The step comes from a second function: here it’s 4 — 3, 7, 0, 4; another key gets a different one

frames.text: size 11 is prime: the step visits everything

slides.title: Robin Hood
slides.main: A key that wandered farther from home takes the slot from the “rich”.

captions: Each key remembers distance d to its home slot (8 % 8 = 0, 2 % 8 = 2 …)
24 % 8 = 0: go 0, 1, 2 — at slot 2 we are d = 2 away, its owner only 0
The rich owner (d = 0) yields: 24 sits in slot 2, key 2 moves on
Key 2 found slot 4 (d = 2): max distance is 2, no longer growing

slides.title: Cuckoo hashing
slides.main: Lookup — at most two probes in the worst case.

captions: Two tables and two functions: each key has exactly two possible homes (A: T1[1] or T2[3], B: T1[1] or T2[0])
A takes its first home — T1[1]
B wants T1[1] too: evicts A, and A moves to its second home — T2[3]
Look up A: checked T1[1] — B is there, T2[3] — found. At most two probes

slides.title: Growth and rehashing
slides.sub: Keep the load factor under control
slides.main: The address depends on size: on growth all keys are reinserted — amortized O(1).

captions: Size 4, keys 4, 9, 6 (mod 4): load factor α = 0.75
Fourth key 11: α = 1 > 0.75 — time to grow the table
The address depends on size: reinsert all keys — rehashing
Size 8: key 4 moved from slot 0 to 4, 6 — from 2 to 6. Rare but costly; amortized O(1)

slides.title: What keys are needed
slides.main: Equal keys — equal hashes; don’t mutate a key while it’s in the table.

captions: If keys are equal, their hashes must match — otherwise the key gets lost
A list key was mutated in place: new hash, we look in the wrong place
Crafted keys with one hash turn the table into a chain: queries become O(n²)

frames.text: attack: all keys in one slot

slides.title: Pattern: counting and grouping
slides.main: Frequencies and groups in one pass — instead of nested loops.

captions: One pass over the data; one table access per item
Key found — add one, not found — store one: frequencies in O(n)
Grouping: the key is computed from the item — anagrams share a key

slides.title: Pattern: complement and prefixes
slides.main: Ask the table: has “target minus current” been seen.

captions: Looking for sum 9: at number 2 the table is empty — remember it
At number 7 ask the table: is 9 − 7 = 2 there? Yes — pair found
Subarrays with sum 3: for each prefix, check if prefix − 3 was seen

slides.title: Pattern: table + list
slides.main: The table finds, the list orders by recency — all in constant time.

captions: The table finds an entry by key, the list keeps recency order
A was accessed: its node moves to the head in one step
D added to a full table: B, the oldest, drops off the tail

slides.title: Rolling hash and frequent items
slides.main: A hash replaces an expensive comparison with a cheap one; real check only on a match.

captions: Pattern “ab”: hash 97 · 31 + 98 = 3105; text windows are computed the same way
Window “xa”: 3817 ≠ 3105 — no need to compare characters
Window “ab”: 3105 matches — only now compare characters for real
Frequent items: bucket k holds items with frequency k — no need to sort everything

slides.title: Summary
slides.sub: What a table can and can’t do
slides.main: Order and ranges aren’t its job: use trees.

captions: Deterministic, fast, uniform; keys immutable, equal keys give equal hashes
Chaining is simple; open addressing is faster on cache; Robin Hood and cuckoo are improvements
Rehashing on passing the threshold — amortized constant
Counting, complement, prefixes with a table, cache, bijection — working patterns
From your own function to your own table and problems on it
